extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) evaluating subject-matter eligibility under Alice/Mayo
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether patent claims recite an 'abstract idea' (e.g., fundamental economic practices, commercial/legal interactions, managing human activity, mental processes) and how to analyze mental-process-type abstract ideas for examiners performing Alice/Mayo step 2A/2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting fundamental economic principles or practices (e.g., hedging risk; managing insurance policies; mitigating settlement risk; financial instruments designed to protect against investment risk; offer-based price optimization; local processing of payments; placing an order based on displayed market information; using advertising as an exchange) are directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and controlling cases cited (e.g., Bilski v. Kappos; Bancorp; Alice; OIP Techs.; Inventor Holdings; Trading Technologies). The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have identified hedging and similar economic practices as 'fundamental economic practice' and therefore unpatentable abstract ideas. Examiner should see listed examples (i–vii) showing diverse economic practices characterized as abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite commercial interactions or legal interactions—agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities, or business relations—are grouped as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: buySAFE (transaction performance guaranty/contractual relationship), Bancorp and Accenture (insurance/contractual processing), Fort Properties (legal obligation/tax-free exchanges), Ultramercial (advertising in exchange for access), Credit Acceptance (processing financing applications), Dealertrack (clearing-house processing). Examiner note: claims 'squarely about creating a contractual relationship' or otherwise about agreements/obligations/marketing/business relations have been treated as abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior, relationships, or interpersonal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to managing human activity, social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions, or interactions between people (e.g., budgeting/setting spending limits; filtering content; voting; providing information without disrupting primary activity; rules for games) are classed as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (budgeting/spending limits), BASCOM (content filtering - abstract at step 2A though step 2B analysis may differ), Voter Verified (voting/verification), Interval Licensing (attention manager), In re Marco Guldenaar (rules for playing games). Examiner should consider these as 'organizing human activity' type abstract ideas and consult cases cited for specific fact patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'mental process' is a concept that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper (observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions), and is considered an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat methods that can be performed mentally or with pen-and-paper as unpatentable abstract ideas (citing CyberSource, Benson, Mayo, Parker v. Flook). The phrase 'mental processes' refers to a type of abstract idea and applies to both product and process claims. Examiners should apply the subsequent sub-points A–D when evaluating whether a claim recites a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: A: Limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind do NOT recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim contains limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind (the human mind is not equipped to perform them), the claim does not recite a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where claims were not mental processes: GPS pseudorange/time calculations (SiRF Tech.), detecting suspicious activity via network monitors/analyzing network packets (SRI Int'l), specific multi-step data encryption methods (Synopsys), halftone image rendering requiring manipulation of computer data structures (Research Corp.). Examiner should assess whether the claimed steps are practically performable mentally; if not, treat as not a mental-process-type abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: B: Claims that encompass a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation can practically be performed in the human mind, with or without a physical aid (e.g., pen and paper, slide rule), the limitation is within the mental processes grouping and the claim recites an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of physical aids to extend memory/capacity does not negate mental nature (cases: Benson; CyberSource; Synopsys; University of Florida; Symantec). Examiners should consult the specification (e.g., whether the claimed map is merely a listing) to determine if the limitation reads on someone performing the steps mentally or with simple aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: C: Claims that require a computer may nevertheless recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may still be an abstract mental process even if claimed as performed on a computer; requiring a computer does not necessarily take a claim out of the mental-process grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must carefully consider the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in light of the specification to determine whether the applicant merely claims a concept performed: (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. If so, the claim is considered to recite a mental process (examples: Benson; Mortgage Grader; Voter Verified; Versata). Subpoint: performing a mental process on a generic computer has been treated as an abstract idea when the underlying steps remain human cognitive actions described at high level.
